exampleAnswers.Purpose and audience: Track claims against source quality, verification state, and next research actions.
exampleAnswers.Working context: This fictional evidence register supports a handover improvement proposal. The entries are sample research tasks, not proof that the claims are true.
exampleAnswers.Example records:
Claim: Owners struggle to identify current files · Evidence needed: Observed lookup tasks · State: In progress · Owner: Maya
Claim: An index improves orientation · Evidence needed: Comparison exercise · State: Not yet tested · Owner: Leo
Claim: The index stays current · Evidence needed: Follow-up maintenance check · State: Not yet tested · Owner: Sam
Claim: Setup effort is manageable · Evidence needed: Timed preparation record · State: Draft record · Owner: Robin
exampleAnswers.Content decisions:
Keep the claim narrow: “An index helps this team find approved files” is easier to evaluate than “indexes improve productivity.” Match the evidence to the actual scope of the claim.
Assess the source: Record where the evidence came from, when it was collected, and what could make it misleading. A persuasive quotation does not replace a relevant method or representative sample.
Use the gaps: The untested maintenance claim is important because the proposed change creates ongoing work. Prioritize that check before presenting the index as a durable solution.
exampleAnswers.Format and interaction: register layout; section navigation and expandable detail where useful; matching portrait document PDF.
exampleAnswers.Sharing and provenance: A hypothetical example informed by Claw Me’s small-team and Agent workflows. These are not Pete’s actual clients, finances, travel plans, research results, or commitments. Keep the real adaptation private until the owner chooses to share.
